// Extract input from webhook
const grade = $input.first().json.body.grade;
const letter = $input.first().json.body.letter.toLowerCase();

// ============================================
// FORM B - Structure Rules
// ============================================
const formB = `FORM B
This is FORM B.
Codes for Major Lesson Parts
Major Part 1: Handwriting/Spelling

Structure of Major Part 1 Handwriting/Spelling 

- Standards 
- Objectives
- Materials
- Scripted Lesson Plan for Handwriting & Spelling 

Subsection D: Scripted Lesson Plan for Handwriting & Spelling 

- Review & Connect: Quote the following verbatim to the User every time: "The purpose of this part of the lesson is to start with a quick review of previously learned sounds. Do not use sounds that have not been directly taught. Do not use words that have sounds that have not been directly taught."
- Model, Explain & Engage: Quote the following verbatim to the User every time: "The purpose of this part of the lesson is to connect a sound or sound patterns that you focused on during your reading block to writing its corresponding grapheme patterns. First, make sure children clearly can distinguish the targeted sound; then, hook that sound to the letter patterns through modeling and explaining the sequence of strokes for letters and correct order of letters."
- Guided Practice: Quote the following verbatim to the User every time: "The purpose of this part of the lesson is to give children practice writing the letter while supporting proper pencil grip and correct sequence of stroke formation using handwriting lines."
- Application: Quote the following verbatim to the User every time: "The purpose of this part of the lesson is to facilitate children's spelling of the letter or letter patterns when they hear the sound (s). This supports children's early coordination of matching sound to letter(s) for the purpose of spelling words"
- Wrap-Up: Quote the following verbatim to the User every time: "The purpose of this part of the lesson is to remind students what they were focused on and provide praise for their accomplishments"

All 5 Subsections of "Section D: Scripted Lesson Plan for Handwriting & Spelling" will have the following components:

Explanation = AI explains the parts of the lesson. Set apart in brackets [ ].
Teacher Script = Detailed example of what the teacher actually says as a rehearsal of the lesson. Set apart with #.
Child Response = ( ) = Expected child response within the script will be set off in parentheses.
Teacher Does = { } = What the teacher is doing within the script will be set off in curly brackets, also called braces.
Gesture = a mnemonic device to support children's memory of a phoneme. Set apart with +
Sequence Verbal Cues: verbal representations of the sequence of strokes for all letters in the alphabet. Set apart with ##Sequence Verbal Cues.
Modification = At the end of a lesson, AI prompts the teacher to ask for additional modifications. Set apart with *
Modification Prompt = *Adaptation: Let me know if you would like any modifications to the lesson`;

// ============================================
// FORM C - Example Output
// ============================================
const formC = `This is Form C.

#Input: 
Objective = letter sound and writing letter z 
Grade = PreK 

#Output:

Handwriting & Spelling Lesson 

A. Standards 

ELAGSEKRF3a: Demonstrate basic knowledge of letter-sound correspondences by producing the primary sound for each consonant. ELAGSEKL1a: Print many upper- and lowercase letters. ELAGSEKL2c: Write a letter or letters for most consonant and short-vowel sounds (phonemes).

B. Objectives 
Pronounce the /z/ sound correctly
Isolate the /z/ sound at the beginning of spoken words. Write the corresponding letter z to represent the /z/ sound. Form uppercase and lowercase z using correct stroke sequence.

C. Materials 
- Zebra sound cards (for sound hunt & gesture-based cues)
- Sound wall or letter-sound anchor chart
- Mini whiteboards and dry-erase markers
- Dotted handwriting worksheets (uppercase and lowercase z)
- Pencils and handwriting paper
- Visual chart showing correct letter formation with cues
- Letter sorting cards or letter manipulatives
- Sound-Letter Hunt worksheet with scaffolded visual supports

1. Review & Connect

[Explanation: "The purpose of this part of the lesson is to start with a quick review of previously learned sounds. Do not use sounds that have not been directly taught. Do not use words that have sounds that have not been directly taught."] (Quote the explanation word for word)

#Teacher Script:
"Let's review our sounds. We are doing our Sound Sparks game. Look up here. When I point to a sound. You will all say that sound when I say go, and when you see my hand close to a fist."
"Ready. My Turn. {Teacher points to /m/.}
Get Ready. Go." (children chorally respond /m/). 
Ready. My Turn. {Teacher points to /a/} 
Get Ready. Go." (children chorally respond /a/). 
{Teacher continues this process, reviewing previous sounds}

2. Model, Explain, Engage
[Explanation: The purpose of this part of the lesson is to connect a sound or sound patterns that you focused on during your reading block to writing its corresponding grapheme patterns. First, make sure children clearly can distinguish the targeted sound; then, hook that sound to the letter patterns through modeling and explaining the sequence of strokes for letters and correct order of letters.] (Quote the explanation word for word)

#Teacher Script:
We've been working on the /z/ sound.
My turn. Listen to my sound /z/.
Put your hand on your vocal box–now say the sound /z/.
Did you feel your vocal box? (Children should respond yes) 
That means you are using your voice, so we use our voice to make the /z/ sound. 
Where are your lips when you make the sound?" (Children expected to say something like opened).
Right, you part your lips and your mouth is spread.
And where is your tongue? (Children expected to say top).
Yes, the top of your month and slightly behind your teeth.
Let's do our sound motion. Get Ready Go. (children use the buzzing bee gesture while saying /z/. +Gesture: Move hand in a zigzag motion through the air while making the /z/ sound).
Let's try. My turn. /z/. Jenna, get ready. Go." (child pronounces /z/ sound)
{The teacher has each child in the group demonstrate the correct pronunciation and provides correction if necessary; if this is a whole group lesson, the teacher has all children repeat first. Then, the teacher will call on a few children who may need extra support}.

Great! Now we are going to play our Sound Hunt Game. Each of you has a zebra card because zebra starts with the /z/ sound. We are listening for the /z/ sound at the beginning of the word. I will say a word, and if you hear the /z/ sound at the beginning, I want you to lift up your zebra card when I say go. If you don't hear it, do not lift up the card. 
My turn. The word is zebra. Get Ready...Go. (children should have lifted the zebra card). Right. Everyone should have lifted the card because zebra begins with /z/. Alright put your listening ears on. My turn. The word is tiger. Get Ready…Go. (children should not have lifted their card). {Teacher repeats this process to cement sound to memory then connects to letter form} 

Wonderful! The letter that matches the /z/ sound – is the letter z. Watch me closely. I will show you how to form uppercase Z then lower case z. No one is using their pencil yet or writing. You are watching me. 
{teacher demonstrates on a visual that shows children the correct sequence of letter strokes and uses sequence verbal cues}.
##Sequence Verbal Cues for letter z: Little line across. Slant down the stairs. Little line across.
First, start at the top line. Little line across. Next, slant down the stairs. And then a little line across. 1, 2, 3 lines.
Say it with me as you watch. 
Start at the top line. Say It. (children repeat).
Little line across. Say it. (children repeat).
Slant down the stairs. Say It (children repeat). 
Little line across. (children repeat).
Let's Count. Ready. Go. (Children count 1, 2, 3 lines).
{Teacher repeats this process for lowercase z–drawing children's attention to where lowercase z starts, on the dotted middle line.} 
What is different from where I started my uppercase Z and where I started lower case z? (Children expected to say at the the top or middle line) 
Exactly, where I start the line. Uppercase Z starts at the top line. Lowercase z starts at the middle dotted line. What's the same about both these letters? (Children expected to notice that they are both formed with three lines that are the same)
Right. They both have the same three line strokes; one just starts at the top, the other starts at the middle dotted line. 

3. Guided Practice 
[Explanation: The purpose is to give children practice writing the letter while supporting proper pencil grip and correct sequence of stroke formation using handwriting lines.] (Quote the explanation word for word)

#Teacher Script:
Let's practice how to write uppercase letter z first. We are not using our pencils yet. Let's do our Magic Finger Write. Place your finger at the top of the line. Let me see {teacher checks students finger placement} Remember it's important when we are writing to try to touch the lines. The lines are there to help us.
Little line across. (children move finger across) 
Slant down the stairs. (children move finger in a slant downwards) 
Little line across. (children move finger across) 
{Teacher has students do that a few times and repeat for lowercase z}. 
Now, pick up the pencil. Show me how you hold your pencil. Remember we slant our paper. Your free hand holds the paper. 
Let's do our Trace & Say. I have dotted lines for you to trace. We are doing uppercase Z first {Teacher points to uppercase Z}. Where do we start if we want to write uppercase Z? (children should say the top line). Yes. Everyone put your pencil at the top line on the left. You want to start here. {Teacher points to top left-hand line} Let me see. {Teacher corrects students if needed}. Ready. Write and say. Go. (Children write using dotted lines as guides and say the sequence verbal cues: "Little line across. Slant down the stairs. Little line across."
Now you do one using the dotted lines. {Teacher monitors children's letter writing}. 
Do one more using the dotted lines {Teacher monitors and repeats process for lowercase z}. 

4. Application 
[Explanation: The purpose of this part of the lesson is to facilitate children's spelling of the letter or letter patterns when they hear the sound(s). This supports children's early coordination of matching sound to letter(s) for the purpose of spelling words.] (Quote the explanation word for word)

#Teacher Script:
Boys and girls, I am going back to the /z/ Sound Hunt game, but now it's the Sound-Letter Hunt game. I am going to say a word. You are listening to the beginning sound of that word. You are going to write the letter of the sound you hear in the beginning of the word. Let me show you. My turn. The word is apple. So I am thinking the beginning sound of "apple" is /a/. I know that the /a/ sound is written with the letter a. I am going to look at my handwriting Sound-Letter Hunt worksheet. {Teacher directs students' attention to the handwriting sound-hunt worksheet. The worksheet displays some previously learned letter-sounds along with the new targeted letter-sound. The handout shows the proper way to write those letters and dotted lines for children to use as guides}
I see letter a. Now I am going to look to find letter a on my paper. I am going to look at how to write the letter a. Then, I am going to use the dotted lines to write the letter a. 
Okay are you ready? Listen. My turn. The word is zebra. Get ready. Go. (children should hear the sound /z/ and write the letter z). {Teacher uses the same list of words that were used in the Sound Hunt activity above. Teacher monitors students' answers providing corrective feedback.}

5. Wrap-Up
[Explanation: The purpose of this part of the lesson is to remind students what they were focused on and provide praise for their accomplishments]. (Quote the explanation word for word)

#Teacher Script:
Alright, boys and girls I am so proud of you. What sound have we been working on? {Teacher holds up zebra sound card] (Children respond /z/). 
Perfect! And which of these letters say /z/ {Teacher provides children with a choice} (Children can touch the correct letter that is displayed in small groups, or the teacher can call on a student to circle the correct letter for the whole class).
Show me how to write it (children air write with sequence verbal cues–e.g., little line across, slant down the stairs, little line across) 
Wonderful! Kiss your brains.`;

// ============================================
// FORM D - Scaffolded Activities
// ============================================
const formD = `FORM D

This is FORM D.

Suggested Activities For Handwriting & Spelling 

Review & Connect Activities 

Tap that sound: Children can keep sticky notes with the sound on it –/a/, /s/. Before beginning a new lesson have children stick some of their sound cards on their desk. The teacher provides the sound and children tap the correct sound card. (low-level)
Sound Spark: The teacher points to a sound card and children must chorally pronounce the sound. (low-level)
Sound Detective: Children focus on listening to the beginning, middle, or end sound. The teacher says a word and indicates to children where in the word they should listen for that sound. Children then point to the correct sound. (middle-level)
Write the sound: The teacher says a sound, and children write the letter that corresponds to that sound on a mini whiteboard. This can also be done with writing the sound at the beginning, middle, and end for more advanced students. (high-level)
How many sounds: The teacher says a word. Children use a manipulative to count and show how many sounds. This activity should be used for children at more advanced stages of phonemic awareness. (high-level)
Sort the sound: The teacher says a sound and children sort by either voiced or unvoiced, continuous or stops. (high-level)

Model, Explain, Engage Activities 

Tap that Sound: Same as Review & Connect but include new targeted sound (low-level) 
Sound Spark: Same as Review & Connect but include new targeted sound (low-level)
Sound Hunt: Teacher says words; children must listen to beginning, middle, or end sound to identify the target phoneme. Children can indicate that they hear target sound by lifting a card with the target sound. (low-level)
Hide-and-Seek Sound: Teacher says words that have the target sound in different positions; it could be at the beginning, middle, or end position. Children must find where the sound is by holding up a beginning, middle, or end card. (middle-level)
Chop-a-Sound: Children are given words with the target sound. They either chop the target sound or another previously learned sound and say what is left. (middle-level)
Sound Puzzle: Children are given two previously learned sounds at a time; they must add in the target sound to create a word. (high-level) 
Sound Switch-a-Roo: Children are given words that include previously learned sounds. They are asked to change a beginning, middle, or end sound by substituting in the new targeted sound. (high-level)
Spell Aloud: Teacher takes previously sound patterns of words and asks children to change a sound to the target sound and spell aloud. (high-level)
Silly Sentence: Teacher asks children to think of words that contain the target sound or sound pattern. Then collaboratively build a sentence using as many of those words as possible. (high-level)
How Many Sounds: Teacher provides children with words that include previously learned sounds and the target sound. Children must segment the sounds in each word. (high-level)

Guided Practice Activities 

Rehearsal of Sequence of Strokes
Finger Run: Children run their finger from left to right across the handwriting lines, pointing to the top, middle, and bottom lines as the teacher names them. (low-level)
Magic Finger Write: Children use their "magic" pointer finger to trace letter shapes on the lines, following the teacher's modeling and verbal stroke cues. (low-level)
Sky Writing: With big arm movements, children write letters in the air while saying the strokes aloud, using shoulders and elbows to build motor memory. (low-level)
Bumpy Road Letters: Children trace textured letter cards (made from sandpaper or raised paint) with their fingers, following the correct stroke path by feel. (low-level)

Writing of the Letters/Words 
Trace & Say: Children trace letters on dotted-line templates with a pencil, saying the strokes aloud. (middle-level)
Start Dot Letters: Letters are printed with start dots and arrows. Children follow the marks to complete each letter step-by-step. (middle-level)
Rainbow Write: Children trace the same letter multiple times with different colored pencils, following correct formation for each layer. (middle-level)
Letter Ladder: A visual with steps for each part of the letter. Children write each step, climbing the "ladder" to finish the full letter. (middle-level)
Top to Bottom Challenge: Children write letters using correct formation, earning a star or check each time they start at the top and follow the correct stroke order. (high-level)
Line Talkers: Children describe how the letter touches the lines. (high-level)
Cover & Try: Children trace a letter, then cover the model and try writing it on their own, focusing on correct sequence and placement. (high-level)
Letter Coach: Children work in pairs—one child "coaches" by checking if the other starts in the right place and follows the stroke order. (high-level)

Application Activities 

Trace the Sound You Hear: Teacher says a sound, but includes multiple opportunities for children to hear the target sound, and children trace the matching letter or letter pattern. (low-level)
Write the Sound You Hear: Teacher says a sound, and children write the matching letter or letter pattern. (low-level)
Sound-Letter Hunt: Teacher says words; children must listen to either the beginning, middle, or end sound to identify the target phoneme. Children then write the corresponding sound they hear. (middle-level) 
Mystery Word Builder: Teacher gives sounds one at a time, and children write each sound as they hear it to form a word. Then they blend and read the completed word. (middle-level)
Sound Switch Writing: Children write a simple word, then change one sound when prompted to create a new word. Focus should be on the target letter-sound. (high-level)
What's that Pattern: Teacher provides children with words that include previously learned sounds and the target sound. Children must segment the sounds in each word and then write the corresponding letter or letter patterns. (high-level)`;

// ============================================
// FORM F - Verbal Cues (All Letters)
// ============================================
const formF = `FORM F
Sequence Verbal Cues

// ============================================
// BUILD SYSTEM PROMPT
// ============================================
const systemPrompt = `You are a structured literacy curriculum expert specializing in the Science of Reading.

Your expertise includes:
- PreK through 1st grade phonics instruction
- Georgia Standards of Excellence (GSE) for English Language Arts
- Handwriting and spelling (transcription) lesson development
- Explicit, systematic phonics instruction

You create detailed, scripted lesson plans that teachers can use directly in their classrooms.`;

// ============================================
// BUILD USER PROMPT
// ============================================
const userPrompt = `Generate a Handwriting & Spelling lesson plan.

## Input Parameters
- Grade: ${grade}
- Target Letter: ${letter}

## Form B: Structure Rules
${formB}

## Form D: Scaffolded Activities
${formD}

## Form F: Sequence Verbal Cues
${formF}

## Form C: Example Output
Use this as a reference for the expected format and structure:
${formC}

## Generation Instructions

1. Follow the exact structure defined in Form B
2. Include all required sections: Standards, Objectives, Materials, and the 5 lesson parts
3. Use the verbatim explanations for each lesson part as specified in Form B
4. Use the correct Sequence Verbal Cues from Form F for the target letter "${letter}"
5. Select age-appropriate activities from Form D based on the grade level "${grade}"
6. Use all required markers:
   - [Explanation: ...] for lesson part explanations
   - #Teacher Script: for teacher dialogue
   - (Children...) for expected child responses
   - {Teacher...} for teacher actions
   - +Gesture: for phoneme gestures
   - ##Sequence Verbal Cues for letter formation instructions
   - *Adaptation: at the end for modification prompt
7. Generate Georgia Standards of Excellence codes appropriate for ${grade}
8. Match the style and detail level shown in Form C

Generate the complete lesson plan now.`;

return [{
  json: {
    grade: grade,
    letter: letter,
    systemPrompt: systemPrompt,
    userPrompt: userPrompt
  }
}];

parameters.jsonBody: ={{ JSON.stringify({ model: 'gpt-4o', temperature: 0.7, messages: [ { role: 'system', content: $('Build Prompt').item.json.systemPrompt }, { role: 'user', content: $('Build Prompt').item.json.userPrompt } ] }) }}
